Well, let me think about this year. I'm 64 now, been doing this wheat-maize rotation for 45 years on my 19 mu of land here in Quzhou. Just me in the household now — my wife passed a few years back, and the kids are off working in Shijiazhuang. So all the decisions are on my shoulders, and all the labor too, though my back isn't what it used to be.

For the wheat, I'll stick with what I know. I've been planting the improved variety — not the newest hybrid, but the one that's reliable. I save some seed but I usually buy fresh every couple of years to keep the vigor up. I'll plant in the first week of October, same as always. The soil's decent, not great — I've farmed this land long enough to know where the low spots are.

The extension fella came by last year and said 15 kg of nitrogen per mu was plenty for wheat, but honestly, I've been putting down closer to 18 kg and my yields are better than most around here. I'm middle-educated, I can read the bags, but 45 years tells me more than any pamphlet. I'll do a base dressing of compound fertilizer before planting — about 25 kg per mu of the 15-15-15 — and then topdress with urea at jointing, around 10 kg per mu. That gives me roughly 18-19 kg N total, plus some P and K. I know it's a bit more than recommended, but I'd rather waste a little money on extra fertilizer than risk a bad yield. A bad year hurts more than a good year helps, that's what I learned in '97 and again in 2012.

For irrigation, I'll water three times for wheat: once right after planting to get it germinated well before winter, once at jointing in March-April, and once at grain filling in May. The well water isn't free — metered electricity for the pump runs me about 20 yuan per mu per time — but three times is what it takes here. Some years I can skip one if we get good rain, but you can't count on rain in the North China Plain.

Now for maize — this is where the crunch comes. Wheat harvest is usually around June 8-12, and I need that maize in the ground almost immediately. The turnaround is brutal, sometimes less than a week. I hire a combine for wheat harvest — I can't swing a scythe like I used to at 64 — and then I either do shallow tillage or sometimes just plant right into the stubble if time is tight. Last year I managed to get it planted by June 15th. I'll use hybrid maize seed, have to buy it fresh every year since saved hybrid seed doesn't breed true. Costs more — about 25 yuan per mu — but the yield difference pays for itself.

For maize fertilizer, I'll put compound fertilizer in the furrow at planting, maybe 20 kg per mu, and then topdress urea at the big trumpet stage — that's the critical time. Total N around 16 kg per mu. Maize needs less fussing than wheat, but if it's dry at tasseling, I'll irrigate. Probably twice for maize: once at big trumpet if it's dry, and once at grain filling. Some years once is enough, some years I need two. I'll budget for two.

Pesticides — I'll spray herbicide on both crops. For wheat, maybe a fungicide too if I see rust. For maize, mainly herbicide and maybe insecticide if the corn borer is bad. My neighbor had borer problems two years ago so I'm watching for that.

Labor is my biggest constraint. Just me, 64 years old, on 19 mu. I can handle the day-to-day — fertilizer spreading, irrigation, spraying — but for harvest and the rush planting after wheat, I hire help. I'll need maybe 8-10 days of hired labor through the year, mostly in June and October. Costs about 120 yuan per day now. My nephew sometimes helps for a day or two when he's back, which saves me a bit.

I keep some cash reserve — I'm not going to spend every yuan on inputs. The pension is only 150 yuan a month, so I need to be careful. Total input costs will run me maybe 7,000-8,000 yuan for the year. That sounds like a lot, but if wheat gives me 450 kg per mu and maize gives me 500 kg per mu, I'll come out fine. Wheat prices have been around 2.4 yuan per kg, maize around 2.2 — do the math, it's worth it.
